name: artificialintelligenceact.eu Article 50: Transparency Obligations
title: artificialintelligenceact.eu Article 50: Transparency Obligations
answer: This source is the artificialintelligenceact.eu page for Article 50 of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. It sets out transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems. Its most useful point for media readers is that providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark outputs in a machine-readable format and make them detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, while deployers of deep fake content must disclose that it has been artificially generated or manipulated. The supplied text is partial and cuts off in several places.

sections.body: This is a page on artificialintelligenceact.eu presenting Article 50 of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. It is a legal text page, with the article's paragraphs and cross references to other articles such as Article 59, Article 60a, Article 80 and Article 111. Its scope is transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems. The supplied copy was harvested on 26 September 2026. The page does not state an author or a publication date.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Article 50 addresses transparency obligations. It says providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, taking into account the circumstances and context of use. It then addresses providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content. Those providers must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Their technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of various content types and the costs of implementation. The article also addresses deployers of emotion recognition systems and biometric categorisation systems, though the supplied text cuts off before the full obligation. It says deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, with an exception where the use is authorised by law. Paragraphs 1 to 4 do not affect Chapter III requirements and are without prejudice to other transparency obligations in Union or national law for deployers. The Commission shall encourage and facilitate codes of practice at Union level for detection, marking and labelling of artificially generated or manipulated content, and shall assess whether adherence to those codes of practice, taking utmost account of the Board's opinion. The supplied text cuts off in several places.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source gives these specific references: Article 50, Article 3(1), Article 3(34), Article 3(39), Article 3(60), Article 59, Article 60a, Article 80, Article 111, Chapter III, and paragraphs 1 to 4. It defines an AI system as a machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that infers from input how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions. It defines a deep fake as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful. It defines biometric data as personal data resulting from specific technical processing relating to physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics of a natural person, such as facial images or dactyloscopic data. It also states that providers must mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable format and that deployers must disclose deep fakes. No percentages or monetary figures appear.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in media would use this source to see the article's wording on synthetic content and deep fakes. It is relevant because it states that providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark outputs in a machine-readable format and make them detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. It also states that deployers of deep fake image, audio or video content must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. For media work that uses or distributes such content, the source is a primary reference for the transparency duties it describes. It does not itself discuss newsrooms, publishing or editorial workflows.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Media

sections.body: The supplied text is partial. Several sentences end mid-word or mid-clause, including the exception for law enforcement uses and the Commission's assessment of codes of practice. The page does not give penalties, compliance deadlines, enforcement procedures or practical guidance for media publishers. It is a legal text page rather than a commercial product, and no author or publication date is stated. It also does not state how the obligations apply to publishers specifically or outside the EU.
